## This deck {.center}

### Eight steps, from a CDC download to `masld_analytic.rds`

**Every step answers the same four questions.** That repetition is the point.

::: {.notes}
(1 min) Timing: per-slide markers sum to about 55 minutes, so this fits a single seminar
slot with room for questions. It is a companion to `reproduction/COHORT_BUILD_STEPS.md` —
the page has more detail on every slide here, and students should read it after, not
during. If you are short on time, the droppable slides are the component table, the
covariates step, and the second half of the ledger.
:::

## The question this deck answers

You have a published Methods section. You have CDC's website. **How do you get from one
to the other, and how do you defend every choice you made on the way?**

- The paper: Kueh MTW et al., *BMJ Open* 2026;16:e113719 — body weight phenotypes and
  mortality in MASLD, NHANES 2007–2018
- The code: `reproduction/R/00_setup.R` → `01_download.R` → `02_build_analytic.R`
- The destination: **6,371 rows**, against a published **6,300**

> The gap is not a failure. **Being able to say why it exists is the skill.**

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Say the last line twice. Students arrive believing a replication succeeds when
the numbers match. Set the opposite expectation now: an unexplained exact match is worth
less than a traced discrepancy, because the exact match might be luck and you would never
know.
:::

## The one habit

A Methods sentence is **not** code. Between the sentence and the code there is always a
decision — and in a published paper the decision is almost always invisible.

::: {.callout-important}
Your job at P1 is not to guess the authors' decision.
It is to **make your own, write down why, and count what it cost.**
:::

Every step in this deck has the same four lines:

1. **What the paper says** — quoted, verbatim
2. **Component → variables** — what that sentence forces you to download
3. **The decision** — and *why*, because the sentence did not fully determine it
4. **N afterwards** — and the *type* of the loss

::: {.notes}
(3 min) This slide is the spine of the whole session. Tell them the four-line shape will
repeat eight times and that they should be able to produce it for their own paper by P1.
The word "cost" matters: a decision with no counted consequence has not been made
carefully.
:::

## Three scripts, one of which matters

| Script | What it decides | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `00_setup.R` | 6 cycles, 18 component names, folder paths. **No analysis switch.** | nothing |
| `01_download.R` | nothing analytic — fetches raw files, records a manifest | `data/raw/`, `_download_manifest.csv` |
| **`02_build_analytic.R`** | **everything**: merge → FLI → MASLD → groups → mortality → funnel | `masld_analytic.rds`, `sample_funnel.csv` |

- Cycle letters used throughout: **E** 07-08 · **F** 09-10 · **G** 11-12 · **H** 13-14 ·
  **I** 15-16 · **J** 17-18
- The *file* carries the suffix (`BMX_H.xpt`); the *variable* usually does not (`BMXBMI`
  in all six)

::: {.notes}
(2 min) The asymmetry is worth naming out loud: two of the three scripts are plumbing.
When a number disagrees with the paper, `02_build_analytic.R` is where you look, and
almost always in the filter chain rather than in the arithmetic.
:::

## Where we are going: the funnel {.dense}

| Step | Criterion | N | Type |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 0 | All NHANES 2007–2018 records | 59,842 | — |
| 1 | Age ≥ 18 | 36,580 | ELIGIBILITY |
| 2 | FLI computable | 14,989 | DESIGN + MISSINGNESS |
| 3 | Hepatic steatosis (FLI ≥ 60) | 6,376 | TARGET POPULATION |
| 4 | MASLD (≥ 1 cardiometabolic criterion) | 6,374 | TARGET POPULATION |
| 5 | Phenotype group assignable | 6,374 | MISSINGNESS |
| 6 | Mortality-eligible and linked | **6,371** | OUTCOME ASCERTAINMENT |
| 7 | Alcohol exclusion applied = FALSE | 6,371 | SWITCH |

**Every row carries a type.** A funnel shows N falling; it does not show *why*.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Show the destination before the journey so nobody is lost in the middle. Then ask
the room: which of these rows is missing data? Most will say "all the ones after step 1".
The answer is: step 2 partly, step 5, and step 6 — and the biggest drops are not missing
data at all. Hold the answer until the DESIGN slide.
:::

# Step 0 — What you download {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Three downloads

| # | What | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 18 components × 6 cycles, from `wwwn.cdc.gov/.../DataFiles/<COMP>_<suffix>.xpt` | 108 files |
| 2 | Multum drug lexicon `RXQ_DRUG.xpt` — tried at 2015, 2017, 2013 | **0 — all three 404** |
| 3 | Linked mortality, `ftp.cdc.gov/.../NHANES_<cycle>_MORT_2019_PUBLIC.dat` | 6 files |

About **204 MB**. Every URL, byte size and status is in `data/raw/_download_manifest.csv`.

::: {.callout-note}
**Why keep a download that 404s?** The lexicon was meant to classify medications by
therapeutic class. It is gone, so the medication covariates fall back to questionnaire
self-report. Deleting the failed download would hide that. **Three `MISSING` rows in the
manifest are the honest record that a planned covariate was never built.**
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) The manifest is the first thing to check when a number moves unexpectedly between
runs. The callout is a reproducibility lesson students under-rate: a pipeline that records
its own failures is worth more than one that silently succeeds with less data.
:::

## Which component supplies what {.dense}

| Component | Key variables | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| `DEMO` | `RIDAGEYR` `RIAGENDR` `RIDRETH3` `INDFMPIR` `WTINT2YR` `SDMVPSU` `SDMVSTRA` | age, Asian cut, PIR |
| `BMX` | `BMXBMI` `BMXWAIST` `BMXHT` | FLI, adiposity, **both group axes** |
| `TRIGLY` | `LBXTR` `LBDLDL` **`WTSAF2YR`** | FLI, TG criterion, fasting frame |
| `BIOPRO` | `LBXSGTSI` (GGT) `LBXSCR` | FLI, eGFR |
| `GLU` `GHB` `HDL` | `LBXGLU` `LBXGH` `LBDHDD` | glycaemia + HDL criteria |
| `BPX` `BPQ` `DIQ` | `BPXSY1-4` `BPXDI1-4`, `BPQ050A` `BPQ100D`, `DIQ010/050/070` | BP criterion, "treatment" arms |
| `ALQ` | `ALQ130` `ALQ120Q` `ALQ120U` `ALQ121` | alcohol exclusion |
| `MCQ` `ALB_CR` `SMQ` `PAQ` | `MCQ160*` `URDACT` `SMQ020/040` `PAD680` | comorbidities, CKD, Model 2 |
| `RXQ_RX` | — | **nothing. Downloaded, never read.** |

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Droppable if short on time. The one line to say aloud is the last row: the
pipeline downloads a file it never opens, and that is documented rather than tidied away.
Point at `BMX` too — three variables from one component drive the FLI *and* both axes of
the exposure, which is the circularity problem that comes back in M1.
:::

## The merge, and the trap inside it

`read_component()` stacks a component across all six cycles and **pads any variable
absent from a cycle with `NA`**. Then 16 `left_join`s onto `DEMO` by `SEQN`.

**N after merge: 59,842.** Safe here: `SEQN` is unique across all six cycles (verified,
zero duplicates), and no joined component has more than one row per person.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Padding makes "never asked" look identical to "did not answer"
| Variable | What it measures (CDC label) | In | So what |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RIDRETH3` | race/ethnicity **with a non-Hispanic Asian category** | G–J | Asian status unknowable for 2007–2010 → Step 5 |
| `DIQ070` | takes diabetic **pills** to lower blood sugar | F–J | in E, "antidiabetic" collapses to insulin (`DIQ050`) alone |
| `MCQ160O` | ever told you had **COPD** | H–J | its % has a different denominator from every other Table 1 row |
| `URDACT` | **albumin:creatinine ratio**, mg/g | F–J | in E, ACR falls back to `URXUMA/URXUCR×100` |
| `ALQ120Q` `ALQ120U` `ALQ101` | how **often** you drink · the **unit** that is counted in · "≥12 drinks in a year?" | E–I | retired in the 2017-18 ALQ redesign |
| `ALQ121` `ALQ111` | the same frequency as **one coded item** · "ever had a drink?" | J | the replacements — different coding, must be harmonised |
:::

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is the first of the two big NHANES traps. Nothing errors when a variable is
absent — the code runs and gives you a column of NA that looks exactly like nonresponse.
Ask: how would you *detect* this in your own pipeline? Answer: a cycle-availability check
before you trust any prevalence, which is what `VARIABLE_MAP.md` prints.
:::

# Step 1 — Age eligibility {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 1 — the four lines

> **Paper:** "The study inclusion criteria were participants **aged>18 years** with
> evidence of MASLD."

| | |
|---|---|
| **Component → variable** | `DEMO` → `RIDAGEYR` |
| **Code** | `02_build_analytic.R:114`, filter at `:315` |
| **Decision** | `age >= 18` |
| **N** | 59,842 → **36,580** · ELIGIBILITY · 23,262 dropped |

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Read the paper's sentence out loud exactly as printed, including the ">". Let the
room notice it before you do. Someone usually says "that's just a typo for ≥" — which is
the right instinct and, here, the wrong answer. Next slide.
:::

## ⚠ The paper says `>`, the code says `≥`

That is **70 people** — and it is not a PDF artefact. The published PDF contains **24
correctly encoded `≥` characters** (`BMI≥30`, `WHtR≥0.6`, `FLI≥60`, `1≤PIR≤4`). Where the
authors meant "at least", they wrote it. At the age criterion they wrote a plain `>`.

| Rule | N | Deaths | Groups I/II/III/IV | Σ\|dev\| |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| **Paper** | 6,300 | 585 | 386 / 4,541 / 769 / 604 | — |
| `age >= 18` (ours) | 6,371 | 586 | 391 / 4,585 / 787 / 608 | 71 |
| `age > 18` (paper's words) | **6,301** | **585** | 379 / 4,534 / 781 / 607 | **29** |

**Counter-evidence:** the paper's Table 1 mean age is 51.0 (16.6) — which is what `≥ 18`
gives. Strict `> 18` gives 51.4 (16.3). **This is a strong lead, not a settled answer.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Spend time here; it is the best worked example in the deck. Three teaching points.
One: a single character in a Methods sentence moved 70 people. Two: the way to test a
reading is to run both and compare against *several* published numbers, not one. Three —
and this is the hard one — the evidence genuinely conflicts, and the honest write-up says
so rather than picking the flattering number. Ask the room which they would defend in a
paper, and make them give a reason.
:::

# Step 2 — Steatosis via the FLI {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 2 — the Fatty Liver Index

> **Paper:** "A threshold of **FLI≥60** was used to determine the presence of hepatic
> steatosis."

```
       exp(L)
FLI = -------- × 100,   L = 0.953·ln(TG) + 0.139·BMI + 0.718·ln(GGT) + 0.053·WC − 15.745
      1 + exp(L)
```

| Input | Component → variable | Formula wants | NHANES gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triglycerides | `TRIGLY` → `LBXTR` | mg/dL | mg/dL ✓ |
| BMI | `BMX` → `BMXBMI` | kg/m² | kg/m² ✓ |
| GGT | `BIOPRO` → `LBXSGTSI` | U/L | U/L ✓ |
| Waist | `BMX` → `BMXWAIST` | cm | cm ✓ |

**N:** 36,580 → **14,989** (computable) → **6,376** (FLI ≥ 60). Median FLI 85.5 (73.7–94.7).

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Check the units every time, even when they match — that check is 30 seconds and
its absence is a silent factor-of-18 error waiting to happen. Note the cohort sits well
above 60, not bunched at the threshold, so the steatosis cut is not knife-edge here.
:::

## Reserved codes: there is no global rule

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`LBXTR` — a lab measurement**

`77` is a triglyceride of 77 mg/dL.

Stripping `77`/`99` "to be safe" deletes
**real data**.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`ALQ130` — a questionnaire item**

`777` is *refused*, `999` is *don't know*.

Leaving them in turns 9 refusals into
people drinking **777 drinks a day**.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Same-looking digits, opposite meanings — in the same dataset, in the same pipeline.
**The codebook decides, variable by variable.** Check it before you compare a variable
to a number.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) The second big NHANES trap, and the one most likely to appear in a student's own
paper. Nine misclassified refusals would not change this paper's conclusion — say that —
and then say that "it did not matter this time" is not a method. They found it because
they looked.
:::

## ⚠ DESIGN is not missing data

Triglycerides come from the **fasting subsample**, which carries its own weight
`WTSAF2YR`. The paper never says whether it restricted to that subsample.

- **21,618** of the 36,580 adults fall **outside the fasting-weight frame** — most were
  never sampled for it. That is **DESIGN**.
- **792** are inside the frame and still lack an input. That is **MISSINGNESS**.

::: {.callout-warning}
Say "outside the frame", not "never asked to fast" — the weight cannot certify that.
**2,031** carry a weight of exactly 0, and **819** have all four FLI inputs with no valid
weight at all, so they demonstrably *were* measured fasting.
:::

Different problems, different remedies: a **weight and a population sentence** for the
first; **P5's missing-data analysis** for the second. Never their sum.

::: {.callout-note}
The arithmetic does not simply subtract: the full file loses **21,591** here, because the
**819** adults with all four FLI inputs but no fasting weight are kept.
21,618 − 819 + 792 = 21,591.
:::

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Return to the question you asked at the funnel slide. Reading every
post-eligibility drop as attrition gives you a number like 30,532 and a completely wrong
story about data quality. The remedy differs by type, which is why typing the row is not
bookkeeping — it determines what you do next.
:::

## Two row sets, kept apart {.dense}

| Row set | FLI step | Final N | What it is |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Full analytic file** | 14,989 | **6,371** | every adult with all four FLI inputs. Saved as `masld_analytic.rds`; every table in `output/` uses it |
| **Locked domain** | 14,170 | 6,048 | its subset carrying a valid `WTSAF2YR` |

They differ by **323** records, and **neither is an error**.

- The paper does not report using survey weights → **6,371 is what reproduces it**
- A design-aware estimate is only possible on **6,048** → that is **P4's** job
- 6,048 is a *different denominator*, not a correction to 6,371

::: {.callout-warning}
**Quote which row set you mean, every single time you state an N.**
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) This is where students lose marks in P1 and P4 — they compute on one row set and
report the other's N. Insist on the habit: the number never travels without its row set.
:::

# Step 3 — MASLD criteria {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 3 — five criteria, at least one required {.dense}

> **Paper:** "MASLD was defined as the presence of hepatic steatosis, accompanied by at
> least one of the following cardiometabolic criteria…"

| # | Paper | Variables | Our rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| i | BMI≥25 **or** waist >94 (M) / >80 (F) | `BMXBMI` `BMXWAIST` | `bmi>=25` OR waist rule |
| ii | FPG≥5.6 mmol/L **or** HbA1c≥5.7% **or** antidiabetic meds | `LBXGLU` `LBXGH` `DIQ010/050/070` | `LBXGLU>=100` OR `LBXGH>=5.7` OR dx OR tx |
| iii | BP≥130/85 **or** antihypertensive | `BPXSY*` `BPXDI*` `BPQ050A` | `sbp>=130` OR `dbp>=85` OR tx |
| iv | TG≥150 mg/dL **or** lipid-lowering | `LBXTR` `BPQ100D` | `LBXTR>=150` OR tx |
| v | HDL ≤40 (M) / <50 (F) **or** HDL-targeted treatment | `LBDHDD` | `<=40` M, `<50` F — **treatment arm not implementable** |

**N:** 6,376 → **6,374**. Two people.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Walk criterion (v) specifically: the asymmetric ≤/< is the paper's own wording,
transcribed rather than "fixed", and the HDL-treatment clause has no NHANES variable at
all. Naming an unimplementable clause beats quietly folding it into something else.
:::

## Judgment call 1 — is the glucose cut 100 or 100.9?

The paper sets criterion (ii) in **mmol/L**. NHANES `LBXGLU` is in **mg/dL**. Someone has
to convert, and the paper never shows the converted number.

1. Paper: fasting glucose **≥ 5.6 mmol/L**
2. Converted: 5.6 × 18.016 = **100.9 mg/dL**
3. We coded **≥ 100** — the conventional rounding
4. **212 people** have a glucose between 100 and 100.9. Our rule counts them as meeting
   criterion (ii); a strict reading would not
5. So we re-ran MASLD with **≥ 100.9** and counted who falls out: **0 people**

::: {.callout-tip}
## The habit, not the answer
"It's only 0.9 mg/dL, it can't matter" is a **guess**. "I re-ran it and 0 people change
status" is a **finding**. Same decision — but only one of them you can defend to a
reviewer. Quantify first, *then* decide to leave it alone.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Students routinely wave away unit conversions. The point is not that 100 vs 100.9
matters — it demonstrably does not here — but that the only way to know that was to run
it, and running it took one line. Ask them how they would have worded this in a Methods
section. "Fasting glucose >= 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L)" is honest; silently using 100 and
citing 5.6 is not.
:::

## Judgment call 2 — and what Step 3 really did {.dense}

**A missing criterion counts as *not met*, not as *unknown*.** `n_crit` uses
`rowSums(..., na.rm = TRUE)`, so an `NA` contributes 0 — conservative: it can only keep
someone **out** of MASLD, never let someone in. It also barely matters here:

| | |
|---|---:|
| Meet criterion (i), adiposity | **6,329 of 6,371** |
| Meet *exactly one* criterion | 354 |
| …of whom, that one criterion is adiposity | **352** |
| Dropped by this whole step | **2 of 6,376** |

**Why.** FLI is built from BMI and waist, and criterion (i) *tests* BMI and waist — so
selecting on FLI ≥ 60 strongly **enriches** for criterion (i) without requiring it.
(**89** people here have FLI ≥ 60 with BMI < 25; 42 fail criterion (i) outright.) It is
near-automatic by enrichment, so the other four rarely decide anything.

> **Report a filter by its effect, not its definition.** "MASLD required at least one
> cardiometabolic criterion" sounds like work; here it excluded **2 people**.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The most transferable idea in the deck. Students describe filters by their
definitions; readers judge them by their effect, and the two can be wildly different.
Then connect it forward to M1: the exposure (BMI x WHtR) and the case definition (FLI)
share BMI and waist, so this near-automatic criterion is the same circularity showing up
in a different place. If a student asks "is the paper wrong here?" - no. The definition
is the standard one. It just does almost nothing once you have conditioned on FLI.
:::

# Step 4 — Alcohol {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 4 — building the alcohol exclusion

> **Paper:** "Individuals with significant alcohol consumption — defined as more than two
> drinks per day for men and more than one drink per day for women — were excluded."

**The paper says it removed these people, so we built the rule.** Getting it right needs
two codebook checks that are easy to skip.

**1 — "Drinks per day" is frequency × quantity, not `ALQ130`.** `ALQ130` is drinks per
*drinking day*. Three drinks every Saturday gives `ALQ130 = 3` but an average of
**0.4/day**. Thresholding `ALQ130` on its own over-excludes about **2,000** people. So we
rebuild it: **`(ALQ130 × days_per_year) / 365`**, with `ALQ120Q`/`ALQ120U` supplying the
frequency (×52 / ×12 / ×1), and `ALQ121` replacing that pair in 2017-18.

**2 — Strip `777` and `999` before comparing to any number.** They mean *refused* and
*don't know*. Left in, **9 people** here become 777-drinks-a-day heavy drinkers.

That yields a per-person flag, `sig_alcohol`. **427 people in the cohort exceed the
paper's threshold.** Whether we then *drop* them is the next slide.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Two lessons live in this one variable: the wrong-variable error (`ALQ130` alone)
and the reserved-code error (777). Both are only recoverable by reading the codebook,
which is the habit being drilled. Stress that we are still just *building* here - nothing
has been excluded yet. Students conflate "I implemented the criterion" with "I applied
it", and this step separates them on purpose.
:::

## ⚠ We built it — and then did not apply it {.dense}

`APPLY_ALCOHOL_EXCL <- FALSE`, so **no rows are dropped: 6,371 → 6,371.** The flag is
still computed, still saved into `masld_analytic.rds`, and the funnel still logs the
setting — so the choice is *recorded*, not hidden, and flipping one line turns it on.

**Why off: applying the paper's own stated exclusion moves us further from the paper.**

| Cohort | N | Deaths | Σ\|group dev\| |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Paper** | 6,300 | 585 | — |
| Ours, exclusion **off** | 6,371 | 586 | 71 |
| Ours, exclusion **on** (427 dropped) | **5,944** | 546 | **356** |

- `reproduction_report.md` §6 says the +71 gap is "almost entirely the alcohol-exclusion
  ambiguity". **The numbers do not support that** — Step 1's age rule fits far better
- So the paper's Methods and its own reported N **disagree with each other**. We cannot
  resolve that; we can document it, and default to the cohort that reproduces the tables

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The shape to teach: implement what the paper says, test it, and when the test
fails, keep BOTH the implementation and the finding rather than quietly dropping either.
Also be explicit that the bullet about §6 is a correction to our own repository, found by
re-running numbers rather than re-reading prose. Students who catch an error in the course
materials should be rewarded, and saying so here makes that credible.
:::

# Step 5 — The four phenotypes {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 5 — obesity × central adiposity

> **Paper:** "Obesity was defined as **BMI≥30kg/m²** (≥25 for Asians). High central
> adiposity was defined as a **WHtR≥0.6**."

|  | WHtR < 0.6 | WHtR ≥ 0.6 |
|---|---|---|
| **Obese** | **I** — 391 | **II** — 4,585 |
| **Non-obese** | **III** — 787 | **IV** — 608 |

`whtr = BMXWAIST / BMXHT` — both in cm, so the units cancel. Five people sit exactly on
0.6 and count as high, matching `≥`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The check that proves the construction is right
Our per-group BMI medians: **30.9 / 35.2 / 27.6 / 28.8** — identical to all four published
values. That holds *independently* of the N gap.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Teach the move, not the result: when your N disagrees, find a statistic that
isolates the piece you want to test. Group BMI medians test the group construction without
being sensitive to who is in the cohort. That is how you localise a discrepancy instead of
guessing at it.
:::

## ⚠ A cut-point you cannot apply to a third of the cohort

`asian` comes from `RIDRETH3 == 6` — and **`RIDRETH3` does not exist in 2007-08 or
2009-10**. The code recodes the resulting `NA` to 0, i.e. *not Asian*, for **2,322 of
6,371 rows (36%)**.

- Where the variable *does* exist, the Asian rule moves **121 of 250** Asian participants
  into the obese arm. **This rule has real bite.**
- In 2007–2010 the only ethnicity variable is `RIDRETH1`, whose category 5 is "Other Race
  — Including Multi-Racial": it *contains* Asians but cannot isolate them
- 71 cohort members fall in it; only **17** have BMI in [25, 30) — the window where the
  rule changes anything

**So: at most 17 of 6,371 are misgrouped.** The paper states one rule for 2007–2018; the
data support it only for 2011–2018.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The point is not the 17. It is that "we checked, and it is bounded at 17" is a
publishable sentence and silence is not. Ask how they would have found this — the answer
is the cycle-availability check from Step 0, which is why that slide is not housekeeping.
:::

## The paper contradicts itself, and the data settle it

- **Methods text:** obesity = BMI ≥ 30
- **Table 1 and Table 2 column headers:** `BMI≥25 kg/m²` / `BMI<25 kg/m²`

The headers are wrong, and you can prove it without asking the authors: the paper's own
group III and IV BMI medians are **27.6** and **28.8**, sitting in columns labelled
"BMI < 25". Impossible.

Coding to **30** reproduces those medians exactly. Coding to 25 does not.

> Finding an internal contradiction and **resolving it against the data** — rather than
> picking whichever reading you prefer — is exactly what M2 asks for.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) A good confidence-builder late in the session: published papers contain errors,
and a careful reader with the data can adjudicate them. Distinguish this from the age
discrepancy, where the evidence conflicts and honest reporting means saying it is
unresolved. Two different situations, two different write-ups.
:::

# Steps 6–8 {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Step 6 — covariates, where the paper says almost nothing {.dense}

> **Paper:** "The definitions of comorbidities in the NHANES study have been previously
> described." — that is the *entire* specification.

| Derived | Variables | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `htn` | `BPQ020`, `BPXSY*` `BPXDI*` | self-report **or** ≥140/90 |
| `t2dm` | `DIQ010`, `LBXGH` | self-report **or** HbA1c ≥ 6.5 |
| `dyslip` | `BPQ080` `BPQ100D`, `LBDLDL` | self-report **or** meds **or** LDL ≥ 130 |
| `ckd` | `LBXSCR`, `URDACT`/`URXUMA`/`URXUCR` | eGFR < 60 (CKD-EPI 2021) **or** ACR ≥ 30 |
| `pir_cat` | `INDFMPIR` | <1 Low · 1–4 Middle · >4 High |
| `current_smoke` | `SMQ020` `SMQ040` | current **among ever-smokers** |

::: {.callout-warning}
The code comment says these are "**calibrated to reproduce the paper's Table 1
prevalences**". That is fitting a definition to a target — **circular**. Report it as:
*the paper did not specify, we chose X, here is the residual gap* (1–3 points).
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Droppable. If you keep it, the callout is the reason: this is the least defensible
thing in the pipeline, it is disclosed rather than hidden, and students should be able to
recognise the same move in papers they read. Also flag that `current_smoke` is NA for
never-smokers, which silently shrinks Model 2's complete-case N.
:::

## Step 7 — the outcome is not in NHANES

Six fixed-width `.dat` files from NCHS, joined by `SEQN`.

| Field | Columns | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `SEQN` | 1–6 | join key |
| `ELIGSTAT` | 15 | 1 = eligible for linkage |
| `MORTSTAT` | 16 | 0 alive / 1 dead |
| `UCOD_LEADING` | 17–19 | `001` heart … `005` cerebrovascular |
| `PERMTH_EXM` | 46–48 | **the clock** — months from the MEC exam |

**Decision: `PERMTH_EXM`, not `PERMTH_INT`** — the exposure is measured at the MEC exam,
so follow-up starts when the exposure was measured. The paper does not say which it used.

::: {.callout-important}
**Verify the column positions before trusting anything.** A one-column offset corrupts
everything silently. Check: `ELIGSTAT` ∈ {1,2,3}, `MORTSTAT` ∈ {0,1}, `UCOD_LEADING` ∈
1–10, `PERMTH_EXM` ≥ 0, `SEQN` in the cycle's range.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) The fixed-width parse is the step with the worst failure mode in the whole
pipeline: wrong by one column and every model still runs, every table still prints, and
every number is wrong. Give them the five-way sanity check as a habit.
:::

## ⚠ A trap inside our own saved dataset

| Definition | CV deaths |
|---|---:|
| `cv_death` in `masld_analytic.rds` — `ucod_leading ∈ {1, 5}` | **185** |
| Heart only — `ucod_leading == 1` | **158** |
| **The paper** | **158** |

- `README.md` says "diseases-of-heart"; `reproduction_report.md` finding #3 says heart-only
- `04_table2_cox.R:42` quietly defines its own `cv_heart` and uses that, so the published
  Table 2 **is** correct

**If you read the analytic file and use `cv_death`, you will disagree with every table in
this repository.** Use `mortstat == 1 & ucod_leading == 1` until it is fixed.

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Say plainly that this is a live defect in the course materials, not a teaching
device. It is also a good illustration of why a derived column in a saved dataset is more
dangerous than a line of analysis code: the analysis is read, the column is trusted.
:::

## Step 8 — save, and count what you lost

```r
s0 <- dat                                                    # 59,842
s1 <- filter(s0, age >= 18)                                  # 36,580  ELIGIBILITY
s2 <- filter(s1, !is.na(fli))                                # 14,989  DESIGN + MISSINGNESS
s3 <- filter(s2, steatosis == 1)                             #  6,376  TARGET POPULATION
s4 <- filter(s3, masld == 1)                                 #  6,374  TARGET POPULATION
s5 <- filter(s4, !is.na(group))                              #  6,374  MISSINGNESS
s6 <- filter(s5, eligstat == 1, !is.na(mortstat), !is.na(time_yr))   # 6,371  OUTCOME
s7 <- if (APPLY_ALCOHOL_EXCL) filter(s6, sig_alcohol == 0) else s6   # 6,371  SWITCH
```

Two files: `masld_analytic.rds` (6,371 rows) and `merged_all.rds` (all 59,842, pre-filter,
so any step can be re-derived without re-reading the `.xpt` files).

> **ELIGIBILITY · DESIGN · MISSINGNESS · TARGET POPULATION · OUTCOME ASCERTAINMENT** —
> if you cannot name a row's type, you do not yet know what the row means.

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Point at `merged_all.rds`: keeping the pre-filter frame is what lets you answer
"what if we had used > 18?" in one line instead of a 20-minute re-run. Cheap insurance,
and it is why every number in this deck could be checked.
:::

# What it all cost {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## The decisions ledger — where we may differ from the paper {.dense}

| Decision | Why | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| ⚠ Age `>= 18`, paper writes `> 18` | matches the reported mean age | 70 rows; best explanation of the N gap |
| ⚠ Alcohol exclusion **off** | applying it gives 5,944 vs 6,300 | 427 rows; report §6's reason is wrong |
| ⚠ Asian cut only where `RIDRETH3` exists | absent in cycles E, F | ≤ 17 of 6,371 misgrouped |
| ⚠ `cv_death` = heart + cerebrovascular | — | 185 vs the paper's 158 |
| Both row sets kept (6,371 / 6,048) | unweighted paper vs design-aware estimate | 323 rows differ |
| `PERMTH_EXM` as the clock | exposure measured at the MEC exam | 6.76 y vs the paper's 6.9 y |
| Unweighted throughout | the paper reports no weights, strata or PSUs | the design-aware estimate is P4 |

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Four ⚠ rows, and they are not the same kind of thing: two are unresolved readings
of the paper, one is a data limitation, one is a defect on our side. Make students
classify them — that classification is what a Limitations paragraph is actually made of.
:::

## The ledger — decisions the paper left to us {.dense}

| Decision | Why | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| FLI transcribed verbatim, no unit conversion | NHANES already supplies mg/dL, U/L, cm | none |
| No code-stripping in `LBXTR`/`LBXSGTSI` | `77` there is a measurement | would delete real values |
| Strip `777`/`999` in `ALQ130`/`ALQ120Q` | there they *are* refusals | 9 refusals saved |
| Alcohol = frequency × quantity | `ALQ130` is per drinking-day | `ALQ130` alone over-excludes ~2,000 |
| Glucose 100 mg/dL for 5.6 mmol/L | conventional equivalent | 212 in the gap, 0 reclassified |
| Missing criterion = absent | conservative | negligible — 6,329/6,371 already meet (i) |
| NHANES BP averaging, not `rowMeans` | documented CDC rule | 5,523 people's SBP/DBP changed |
| Composite comorbidities | paper cites prior work instead of specifying | 1–3 pt gaps; calibration is circular |

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Droppable. If you keep it, the BP row is the one to dwell on: correcting it moved
5,523 people's blood pressure and the hazard ratios only in the third significant figure.
A coding error can be real, worth fixing, and immaterial to the headline — all at once.
:::

## Did it reproduce?

| | Reproduced | Published |
|---|---|---|
| Analytic N | 6,371 | ~6,300 |
| Groups I/II/III/IV | 391 / 4,585 / 787 / 608 | 386 / 4,541 / 769 / 604 |
| Deaths | 586 | 585 |
| Group BMI medians | 30.9 / 35.2 / 27.6 / 28.8 | **identical** |
| Group IV HR, unadjusted → adjusted | 15.14 → 2.91 | 15.13 → 2.89 |

**Yes — and the residual gap is traceable, not mysterious.**

> Read crudely, Group IV has the poorest survival, and the paper reports that. Read
> adjusted, Groups III and IV are indistinguishable (2.99 vs 2.91). The replication
> succeeds; the disagreement is about **which contrast supports the conclusion**.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) End the analytic content here. The blockquote is the most important sentence in
the whole reproduction: the arithmetic is fine and the interpretation is the problem.
That distinction — reproducible but over-claimed — is the M2 genre in one line.
:::

## For P1

1. **Work the loop, in order:** paper sentence → operational concept → NHANES variable →
   component → *that cycle's* codebook → raw `.xpt` → your code → cohort consequence
2. **Write four lines per step:** the quoted sentence, the component and variables, the
   decision and its reason, the N afterwards
3. **Type every funnel row.** DESIGN, MISSINGNESS and TARGET POPULATION are not
   interchangeable and do not add up
4. **Two decisions here are still open** (age, alcohol). Reproducing a number is not the
   goal — being able to say *why* yours differs is

::: {.callout-tip}
Full detail, with every number and line reference:
**`reproduction/COHORT_BUILD_STEPS.md`**
:::

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Close on item 4. An unexplained exact match is worth less than a discrepancy you
can account for — the same line you opened with. Point them at the page and stop.
:::

## One exercise

Open `data/derived/merged_all.rds` and answer, with code:

1. How many participants are **exactly 18**? What happens to N, deaths, and the four group
   sizes if you use `age > 18`?
2. How many people would the **alcohol exclusion** remove? Does applying it move you
   toward or away from the paper's 6,300?
3. Pick **one** variable from Step 0's availability table. Which cycles is it missing
   from, and what does the NA-padding do to the statistic it feeds?

Write four lines for each: **what the paper says · what you did · why · what it cost.**

::: {.notes}
(2 min) All three are answerable in a few lines against the saved frame, and all three
have answers given in this deck — so students can self-check. Question 3 is the one that
transfers to their own paper, because the specific variable does not matter.
:::
